summary: AYNI HEALTH is a visual health monitoring platform that helps astronauts assess their own health when a doctor is minutes away. On long missions to the Moon or Mars, communication with Earth is delayed and crews must detect physical and mental changes by themselves, without medical training. Our web application records key health indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and radiation dose), shows each one with a color-coded status and explains what it means, how to measure it and what to do next. When a value or symptom signals danger, the system triggers alerts and tells the crew when to contact the flight surgeon or mission control, without making diagnoses. It works offline and syncs when the connection returns. The indicators are organized around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, and every reference range is backed by NASA and medical sources. Our team is based in Cusco, Peru, at 3,400 m, where hypoxia and isolation make a real terrestrial analog. The name ayni comes from the Andean principle of reciprocity: caring for those who care for the mission.
details:
What exactly does it do?

What would you do if you felt chest pain halfway to Mars, with the nearest doctor minutes away? AYNI HEALTH is a health self-assessment tool for crew members who are not medical professionals:

• It records health indicators through simple forms: blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, glucose, sleep, mood (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires), and radiation dose.

•  It shows each indicator with a color-coded status (normal, warning, alert) and trend charts over time.

• It explains how to take each measurement, why it matters in space and when to ask for help.

• It generates automatic alerts and, for serious symptoms such as chest pain or shortness of breath, tells the crew to activate the mission’s emergency procedure and contact the flight surgeon and mission control.

• It includes an interactive body map linked to NASA’s five hazards, an AI assistant that never sends the crew member’s name, and a nutrition plan with Andean foods.

• It keeps working offline and syncs the data when the connection returns.

How does it work?

1. The crew member selects a measurement and follows the step-by-step guide.

2.The value is saved and compared with reference ranges from NASA and medical sources.

3.The dashboard updates the status and the trend, and an alert is created if the value is out of range.

4. The alert explains what to do: repeat the measurement, apply a preventive action, or contact the flight surgeon and mission control.

5. Three roles (administrator, physician and crew member) control who can see and edit the data.

Tested with real data. Besides a 120-day simulated mission (clearly labeled as simulated), the prototype imports real physiological reference data from healthy people on Earth: 32 reference subjects and 75 records from PhysioNet (Non-EEG, BIG IDEAs Lab and MMASH) and CDC NHANES 2021–2023. These records are labeled “real reference data” and are never presented as astronaut data; the same thresholds generated 11 alerts on them. A live connection to NASA DONKI warns the crew about recent solar activity in the radiation module, with an offline fallback. The code passes 173 automated tests, and the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires use their complete validated versions (9 and 7 items).

AYNI Station (designed IoT extension). To measure values instead of only typing them, we designed the AYNI Station: a low-cost, battery-powered station based on an Arduino Mega 2560 with 12 sensing modules (ECG, EMG, pulse oximetry, respiration, tremor, plantar pressure, electronic auscultation, spirometry, galvanic skin response, infrared temperature, ultrasound bone densitometry and Geiger radiation dosimetry), housed in a friendly robot-style enclosure meant to make being measured less stressful. Two modules target spaceflight hazards: bone loss, reported at about 1–1.5% of bone mineral density per month in space (Stavnichuk et al., 2020), and radiation. The station is planned to send each reading to the platform as a short text line (over USB with the Web Serial API, or through a Bluetooth LE or Wi-Fi bridge), where the same thresholds, alerts and escalation rules would apply; this data link is a design and is not yet implemented. The station is an educational prototype, not a certified medical device: it runs only on battery so the person stays electrically isolated, its Geiger counter gives an indicative dose rate rather than calibrated dosimetry, and like the platform it makes no diagnoses. Blood pressure, glucose, sleep and the PHQ-9/GAD-7 questionnaires remain manual entries. We documented its pinout, a firmware draft and a benchtop validation plan in a separate technical report.

The firmware code and that technical report are available in the AYNI Station repository: https://github.com/Elgabo04/iot-code-anyhealth. Figure 1 shows the station design and Figure 2 the visual reference for its robot-style enclosure.

Project timeline. AYNI HEALTH started in October 2026 as a university course project by our team. During the hackathon we focused it on this challenge and added the emergency protocol, verified thresholds backed by NASA and medical sources, NASA-STD-3001 radiation alerts, the NASA DONKI integration and real reference data from PhysioNet and CDC NHANES.

What benefits does it have?

• Autonomy: the crew can understand and act on their health when help from Earth is delayed.

• Safety: clear escalation rules instead of improvised diagnoses.

• Accessibility: plain language, color plus icon and text for every status, and Spanish and English interfaces.

• Low cost: a web application that runs on any device and does not depend on specialized hardware.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, we want to validate the tool with real measurements taken by our team in Cusco, at 3,400 m, a high-altitude analog for hypoxia and isolation. In the long term, the same tool could support health monitoring in remote Andean communities far from medical care, bringing the benefits of space research back to Earth.

For the AYNI Station we plan non-invasive benchtop tests: checking ECG, EMG and skin-conductance signals at rest and during light effort, measuring dense and porous bone phantoms with the ultrasound module, recording natural background radiation and potassium chloride salt with the Geiger counter, and comparing its SpO₂, heart rate and temperature readings with reference devices in Cusco.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

•Languages: JavaScript, JSX, Python (data conversion scripts), SQL, HTML, CSS

• Frontend: React 18, Vite, React Router, TanStack Query, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Framer Motion, Lucide icons

• Backend: Node.js, Express, Sequelize, Zod, JSON Web Tokens, bcrypt, Helmet, Pino

• Database: MySQL (MariaDB compatible)

•  External data: NASA DONKI API, PhysioNet datasets, CDC NHANES

• Offline support: IndexedDB, service worker (Progressive Web App)

• Testing: Vitest, Supertest, Playwright (173 automated tests passing)

• Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, ESLint, Prettier

•   Hardware (AYNI Station design): Arduino Mega 2560, AD8232 (ECG), MyoWare (EMG), MAX30102 (pulse oximeter), NTC thermistor (respiration), MPU6050 (tremor), FSR402 (plantar pressure), electret microphone with LM386 (stethoscope), MPXV7002DP (spirometry), GSR module, MLX90614 (infrared temperature), 1 MHz piezo pair (bone ultrasound), Geiger board with M4011 tube (radiation), SSD1306 OLED display, 7.4 V LiPo battery; firmware in C++ with the Arduino IDE
